articles.title: Query, key, value and scaled attention
articles.concept: Queries represent what a position seeks; keys support matching; values provide content to combine. Scaled dot-product attention turns query-key compatibility into normalized weights and uses them to aggregate values. Attention weights are contextual computation, not a universal explanation of model decisions.
articles.mechanism: Compute query-key dot products, scale by the square root of key dimension, apply masks before softmax and multiply the resulting weights by values. Track the axes explicitly: score matrices relate query positions to key positions, while value width determines the resulting feature width.
articles.boundary: Masking after normalization can leave invalid probability mass or require renormalization. Entirely masked rows need an explicit implementation policy.
articles.example: A two-key example computes a scalar weighted value and verifies that weights sum to one before aggregation.
articles.application: Use an explicit attention calculation to diagnose masking, shape and numerical bugs before comparing optimized implementations.

import math
q=[1,0];keys=[[1,0],[0,1]];values=[10,20]
scores=[sum(a*b for a,b in zip(q,k))/math.sqrt(len(q)) for k in keys]
weights=[math.exp(s-max(scores)) for s in scores]
weights=[x/sum(weights) for x in weights]
assert abs(sum(weights)-1)<1e-12
print(round(sum(w*v for w,v in zip(weights,values)),3))

articles.title: Attention heads, causal masks and KV sharing
articles.concept: Multi-head attention uses several learned projections to represent different interaction patterns. Causal masks prevent a decoder position from reading future positions. Multi-query and grouped-query variants share key/value representations across query heads in different ways to reduce cache and bandwidth requirements.
articles.mechanism: Distinguish query-head count from key/value-head count when estimating inference state. Build masks from the actual query/key position convention, especially when cached prefixes change offsets. Verify that shared representations satisfy the architecture configuration rather than copying assumptions from a standard multi-head diagram.
articles.boundary: More heads do not guarantee better task quality. A valid-looking triangular mask can still be wrong when its coordinates ignore cached-prefix positions.
articles.example: A toy causal mask for three positions allows only the current and earlier keys. A separate accounting exercise compares key/value head counts.
articles.application: Reason about cache size and causal correctness when serving decoder models with different attention architectures.

articles.title: Position information and RoPE
articles.concept: Attention without position information does not inherently encode the order of input tokens. Transformers add or otherwise incorporate position signals. Rotary position embeddings apply position-dependent rotations to query/key components, making relative position differences influence their dot products.
articles.mechanism: Track position indices through prompt formatting, padding and cache reuse. In a two-dimensional rotary pair, a shared rotation preserves a vector norm; differing rotations change relative alignment. Real implementations distribute frequencies over pairs and may use architecture-specific scaling choices.
articles.boundary: Increasing a configuration limit does not prove reliable long-context behavior. Position extrapolation, model training distribution and the serving implementation must be evaluated together.
articles.example: A two-dimensional toy rotation checks norm preservation and a right-angle rotation of a unit vector.
articles.application: Inspect rotary position handling when incremental decoding or long-context behavior differs from a trusted baseline.

articles.title: Encoder, decoder, BERT, GPT and T5
articles.concept: Encoder-only, decoder-only and encoder-decoder families organize attention and training objectives differently. BERT-style encoders are commonly associated with masked-token representation learning; GPT-style decoders use autoregressive prediction; T5-style systems frame tasks as text-to-text sequence transformation.
articles.mechanism: Match architecture to the required input/output contract. Bidirectional encoding can use both sides of a visible input, while autoregressive output positions need causal constraints. Encoder-decoder models separate source representations from a generated target through cross-attention. Actual model variants may depart from the simplified family description.
articles.boundary: Architecture names do not by themselves determine deployment quality, licensing or whether an instruction-following checkpoint exists.
articles.example: A tiny task router selects encoding for semantic representation, decoding for continuation and sequence transformation for source-to-target tasks.
articles.application: Compare model families for embeddings, classification, translation and interactive generation using the same task-level acceptance criteria.

articles.title: Context windows, prefill and decoding
articles.concept: A context window limits the tokens a model can attend to in a request, subject to model and service constraints. Prefill processes the supplied prefix; decoding extends it. KV caching avoids recomputing some prior representations but does not make long prompts or long outputs costless.
articles.mechanism: Measure time to first token and subsequent token latency separately. Budget prompt components and output reservation before accepting a request. Cache state grows with active sequences and context length, so concurrency limits must account for real workload shapes rather than average request counts.
articles.boundary: A nominal context maximum is not a guarantee of uniform evidence use across positions. Evaluate task quality with relevant passages placed at different distances.
articles.example: A token-budget function checks instructions, user input, evidence and reserved output against a declared toy limit.
articles.application: Plan document assistants with measured evidence budgets, explicit truncation policy and serving limits based on long-prompt traffic.

articles.title: Temperature, top-k and top-p sampling
articles.concept: Decoding transforms a model distribution into output choices. Temperature rescales logits, top-k limits a fixed number of candidates and top-p retains a probability-mass nucleus. These are sampling controls, not mechanisms that supply missing factual knowledge or guarantee valid output.
articles.mechanism: Apply a documented sequence of transformations and renormalize the retained mass before sampling. Tie handling, seeds and implementation details affect reproducibility. Compare decoding settings on diversity, correctness and task constraints rather than assuming more randomness is always more creative or useful.
articles.boundary: Temperature zero behavior is implementation-specific; a reproducibility claim should specify the service, model and settings rather than promise identical results everywhere.
articles.example: A nucleus selector retains the smallest descending-probability prefix reaching a target mass, with deterministic tie-breaking.
articles.application: Tune generation policies on a fixed evaluation set and keep critical schema or authorization checks independent from sampling choices.

articles.title: Prompt engineering, examples and reasoning
articles.concept: Prompts specify a task, context and output contract, but they do not replace system permissions or evaluation. Zero-shot instructions and few-shot examples differ in the demonstrations supplied. A useful explanation can show a concise rationale or verifiable calculation without requiring disclosure of private internal chain-of-thought.
articles.mechanism: Separate trusted application instructions from untrusted source text. Choose examples representative of the task, test them on held-out cases and version changes. Ask for evidence, intermediate checkable artifacts or a concise explanation appropriate to the task rather than assuming a longer reasoning transcript is more reliable.
articles.boundary: Few-shot examples can introduce formatting shortcuts or leakage. Strong wording alone cannot enforce a security boundary or guarantee factuality.
articles.example: A toy prompt builder keeps policy, task and source material in separate fields and refuses an oversized source rather than silently erasing instructions.
articles.application: Develop extraction or support prompts with regression tests, evidence references and independently enforced tool permissions.

articles.title: Structured outputs and function calling
articles.concept: Structured outputs target a declared response shape; tool calling proposes an application operation with arguments. Neither valid JSON nor a tool name grants authorization. The host must validate types, business rules, user permissions and side effects before executing a model-proposed action.
articles.mechanism: Parse the response, validate its schema, then perform semantic checks against trusted application state. Derive identity from authentication rather than model arguments. Use allowlisted operations, explicit confirmation for consequential actions and idempotency for retries. Fail safely when output is malformed or requests an unsupported operation.
articles.boundary: A schema-valid amount or object ID can still be unauthorized or nonsensical. Do not confuse syntax constraints with business correctness.
articles.example: A synthetic lookup tool rejects unknown fields and operation names and derives its caller identity outside the generated payload.
articles.application: Use model proposals for bounded retrieval or workflow assistance while enforcing ownership and actions in server-side code.

articles.title: Model comparison, LLaMA and deployment choices
articles.concept: Model selection balances measured task capability, license terms, data handling, hardware, latency and operating cost. Open-weight availability is not identical to unrestricted open-source licensing. A hosted proprietary API and a self-hosted checkpoint expose different operational responsibilities and control surfaces.
articles.mechanism: Freeze a representative evaluation set, prompt format and success criteria before comparing candidates. Record model revisions, tokenizer settings, refusal behavior and workload shape. Assess privacy and licensing from actual terms and deployment design, and separate benchmark capability from product suitability.
articles.boundary: A ranking on an unrelated public benchmark cannot establish the best choice for a particular assistant. Verify licenses and current service terms rather than assuming a model-family name settles them.
articles.example: A toy decision table filters models by required constraints before comparing measured quality and latency, making the trade-off explicit.
articles.application: Choose a model using reproducible workload evaluation and a deployment review that includes maintenance and data boundaries.

questions.title: How does structured output differ from tool execution?
questions.answer:
Structured output constrains a response representation; a tool call requests an operation. The application decides whether and how to execute it.

Parse the response, validate its schema, then perform semantic checks against trusted application state. Derive identity from authentication rather than model arguments. Use allowlisted operations, explicit confirmation for consequential actions and idempotency for retries. Fail safely when output is malformed or requests an unsupported operation.

A schema-valid amount or object ID can still be unauthorized or nonsensical. Do not confuse syntax constraints with business correctness.
questions.conceptual_explanation: Structured outputs target a declared response shape; tool calling proposes an application operation with arguments. Neither valid JSON nor a tool name grants authorization. The host must validate types, business rules, user permissions and side effects before executing a model-proposed action.
